newsitem.title: UK: F0CUS-Littlewoods calls off shop sale.
newsitem.headline: F0CUS-Littlewoods calls off shop sale.

text.p: Britain's privately-owned retail to football pools group Littlewoods said on Monday that it was abandoning plans to sell its retail chain and would instead refocus strategy while selling off selected sites.
"Despite considerable interest in the stores...the board believes there is greater merit in...retaining the division and implementing a revised and radical strategy," the company said in a statement.
Littlewoods, which is owned by the secretive millionaire Moores family, put its retail division up for sale in March.
But it wanted to find one buyer for the entire portfolio of 135 high-street stores, with a suggested price tag upwards of 500 million pounds ($831.1 million).
However, speculation has mounted that the company came under pressure from potential buyers to sell the stores on a piecemeal basis, allowing retailers to pick out the most appropriate sites.
Chairman James Ross said on Monday that "disposal is not the best way to create value".
He added in a statement that the new strategy would "transform the business, significantly enhance profitability and deliver real value to customers and shareholders".
Ross told Reuters he would be disappointed if there were no positive signs from the changed strategy within three years and suggested a turnaround would take five years.

He said the company intended to hold on to over 100 stores and streamline them into units of 10,000-15,000 square feet, with a focus on female consumers over 45 years old who buy for themselves and their partners.

The change in strategy coincides with the appointment of Barry Gibson, retail director at British airport operator BAA Plc, to the post of chief executive after predecessor Bill Huntley retired in May.

The group is awaiting government approval for its 367.5 million pound purchase of mail order group Freeman's from Sears, conditionally agreed in April when the struggling retail group announced a restructuring.
Amid cut-throat competition in the retail market, Sears decided on a demerger and disposals as a way forward. Its chief executive Liam Strong departed in the process.

Ross said Littlewoods aims to realise value by selling selected key properties, for which it said it had "some very interesting offers". But he declined to identify potential buyers. "We have not got to that process yet," he said.
Supermarket groups have been tipped as potential buyers, although market leader Tesco said it was an unlikely bidder of the whole portfolio in April.

Chemist chain Boots and retailer Kingfisher, which owns do-it-yourself chain B&Q, electrical retailer Comet and chemist chain Superdrug, have also been tipped as possible buyers of Littlewood's retail chain and could still be interested in selected stores, analysts said.
The block on a bulk sale is unlikely to have much effect on shares, analysts said.
Kingfisher's shares, which closed 14.5 pence weaker at 681.5 pence on Monday in a lower market -- were largely discounting such a move already on the grounds of cost, they added.
However, selling selected sites, which Littlewoods said would realise value, could prove difficult.
"The best stores will be the ones that Littlewoods wants to retain and the ones that people want to buy," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
"All the industry would cherry-pick the same stores," said Robert Miller of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, adding that Littlewoods need not hurry to sell.

There was also scepticism over the likely success of the new strategy for the stores, which would also aim to build on the group's Berketex higher quality lines, with the possibility of a mail order catalogue for the brand.
"Littlewoods does not get into the good retailer camp at the moment -- they obviously hope to do so but I will wait and see," the analyst said.
($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
